Title: Speech at the commemoration of the 64th anniversary of the Central Bank of the Dominican Republic
CentralBank: Central Bank of the Dominican Republic
text: Speech by Governor Hector Valdez Albizu in the commemoration of the 64th Anniversary of the Central Bank of the Dominican Republic It is a great honor for me to address for the fourteenth time all of you, dear Bancentralians, on the occasion of commemorating the 64th anniversary of the creation of the Central Bank of the Dominican Republic. I confess to you, once again, that living moments like these fills me with special emotion and deep gratitude to God, for guiding my steps and blessing me with an extraordinary family. The unconditional love, support and understanding of my loved ones are essential in the difficult task of serving as the head of this governing institution of the Monetary and Financial System of the Nation, thanks to the trust placed in me by His Excellency the President of the Republic, Dr. Leonel Fernandez Reyna, who has honored me with such high distinction. It is truly not possible to assume this commitment of so much responsibility, without the support of the staff of the Central Bank, who daily strive to give their best to make the "duty accomplished" our greatest service to the Homeland. Precisely in this year, that beautiful bond that unites us as a Bancentralian family has been amply revealed. Without any reservations, their hearts opened to console and wipe away tears of the soul, in very difficult moments and of indescribable pain for those who speak to them, for the loss of a very dear and close relative; as well as for the entire Central Bank, before the departure of endearing and unforgettable co-workers who, as Facundo Cabral said, "went ahead of us", or when we saw the need to raise joint prayers to the Almighty for the health of collaborators and relatives. How much solidarity in the same feeling! But not only in the human part have we been shaken. In the international economic and financial sphere, the aftermath of the global crisis that began at the end of 2007 has continued to impact all nations of the world, with different intensities, generating considerable volatilities in trade and markets, high unemployment rates and significant levels of public and private leverage, among other aspects. Certainly, few economists thought that even four years later we would be feeling the ravages of this crisis, even with the fear that a second recession could ensue, as the Nobel Prize in Economics Joseph Stiglitz has expressed. International Environment At the end of 2010, the main economies of the globe presented encouraging forecasts, however, at this time the international environment shows multiple complexities and challenges. The new obstacles to global economic recovery this time emanate mainly from fiscal and sovereign debt problems, especially in Greece and other countries of the European periphery. The latest projections of the IMF's World Economic Outlook (WEO) suggest that the growth of the world economy would be in the order of 4.0% for both 2011 and 2012. We note that in the case of the United States of America, our largest trading partner, the IMF has revised growth prospects down several times this year. The latest projections of this month of October, suggest that its growth would be around 1.5% in 2011 and 1.8% for 2012, while its labor market would continue to lag. Indeed, the unemployment rate in the United States currently stands at 9.1%, well above the historical average of around 5%, leading to the contemplation of new fiscal and monetary stimulus initiatives, such as a Bill to encourage job creation recently presented by the President of the United States of America, in the midst of a somewhat difficult political environment. On the other hand, the countries of the Euro Zone would grow in the order of 1.6% for 2011 and 1.1% for 2012. While Germany and France maintain more encouraging prospects, countries such as Portugal, Ireland, Italy, Greece and Spain have low growth rates, negative in some cases. To illustrate this significant contrast, it is enough to mention that the unemployment rate in Germany is 6.6%, the lowest since the reunification of that country in 1989, while Spain has a rate of 21.2%, the highest in all of Europe. Despite the difficulties facing the world's major economies, the situation is very different in emerging markets. As Brazil's Finance Minister Guido Mantega pointed out at the recent IMF-World Bank Autumn Meeting in which we participated, "developing economies have become the real engines of global economic growth," which is why the IMF forecasts that economic growth in 2011 and 2012 would be around 9% in China. 7% in India, 6% in Argentina and 5% in Chile, just to mention a few economies. As a whole, the so-called BRIC countries, i.e. Brazil, Russia, India and China, would be growing above 7% in the coming years, while the CIVETS, the new group composed of Colombia, Indonesia, Vietnam, Egypt, Turkey and South Africa, would be growing above 4.5% in the medium term. In the case of Latin America, I agree with Chilean Finance Minister Felipe Larrain, who points out that the region today is part of the solution, not the problem. Despite the uncertainty in the performance of the world's major economies, fortunately Latin America and the Caribbean are well positioned, maintaining a projected growth of 4.5% at the end of 2011 and 4% for 2012, thanks to the implementation of sound macroeconomic policies in the last decade, as well as the stability and adequate capitalization of their banking systems. As you can see, this difficult external panorama with roots in developed nations, continues to be full of uncertainty, since there is still no consensus among economists and international organizations in glimpsing a way out of this complex situation, which is the great challenge that lies ahead in the present decade. Domestic Policy Reaction to the International Crisis In this context and on the threshold of a Digital and Technological Age, which has turned the world into a cyber village, hardly a small and open economy like the Dominican one can be isolated from this global problem. We are increasingly integrated, and our business cycle is therefore influenced by developments in the rest of the world. In this sense, so that economic agents and the general public can measure the scope of domestic policy, in the face of the restrictions derived from the international crisis, I wanted to briefly propose the approach of the strategies promoted by government authorities. As you will recall in 2009, given the unfavorable external situation described, the current Government decided to sign a new Stand-by Agreement with the IMF to protect the national economy, developing a plan of counter-cyclical measures aimed at stimulating economic growth in the short term. Under this scheme, and in the face of minimal inflationary pressures, the Central Bank reduced its policy interest rate by 5.5 percentage points, being the third country in Latin America that most decreased its reference rate, only surpassed by Chile and Colombia. In that sense, the weighted average of the lending bank rate decreased by 14.5 percentage points, from 25.2% in January 2009 to 10.7% in August 2010, with Dominicans accessing loans at interest rates that have turned out to be the lowest in the entire national monetary and financial history. The monetary measures were accompanied by a strong fiscal stimulus until June 2010, within the framework of the Agreement with the IMF. The combined effect of these policies had the expected effect, managing to stimulate consumption and public and private investment, so that GDP expanded at a rate of 3.5% in 2009, the highest in the region, and 7.8% in 2010, consolidating the economic recovery in an environment of low inflation and relative stability of the exchange rate. However, as expected, low interest rates accelerated the private credit of all financial institutions, growing this variable almost twice the rate of nominal GDP, revealing this behavior a potential danger of overheating of the Dominican economy. Adding to this domestic situation, the sustained rise in international prices of oil and other commodities since mid-2010, the need to moderate the pace of growth in domestic demand resurfaced, in order to avoid sharp deviations from the inflation target. Hence, in a proactive manner, if you will, the monetary authorities began the gradual withdrawal of the monetary stimulus implemented to cushion the effects of the global crisis, assuming a more neutral policy stance. Indeed, between October 2010 and May 2011, the Central Bank gradually increased its policy interest rate by 275 basis points, from 4% to 6.75%. These measures, in accordance with the monetary policy transmission mechanism, had effects on market rates, which increased in stages by approximately 5 percentage points during this period, obtaining to date the expected moderation in credit, economic activity and inflation. In the same direction, monetary aggregates have evolved, that is, the money circulating in the economy to sustain the increase in commercial and financial transactions, registering the expanded monetary base an annualized growth rate of 7.2% to September 2011, while credit to the private sector in national currency has slowed from a growth of 20% in October last year to 12.5% at the last available date, as foreseen in the Monetary Programme and in line with the behaviour of nominal GDP and the inflation target. Likewise, total annualized bank credit, which includes financing to the public sector, slowed from 18.1% in October 2010 to 7.3% to date. I think it would be useful and necessary to note, for the edification of economic agents, that this recent behavior of interest rates in the Dominican Republic has been similar to that of other countries in the region. And it is that the monetary policy rate tends to be counter-cyclical, adjusting downwards, assuming an expansionary stance, when a process of significant economic slowdown arises or is glimpsed, while the rate is induced to rise, with a neutral or restrictive approach, in the event of an eventual risk of overheating of the economy that could alter price stability and the deficit in the current account. In the same direction of monetary policy, fiscal policy was moving, moving from an expansionary phase until mid-2010 to a significant adjustment in spending, as shown by the reduction in the central government deficit, going from 3.5% of GDP in 2009 to 2.5% in 2010. This adjustment has continued, so it is expected that at the end of this year this deficit will be reduced to 1.6% of GDP, a truly extraordinary effort if we frame it in the current context of slowdown in the world economy. As this distinguished audience knows, an IMF mission was recently in the country to complete the seventh review of the agreement. After very fruitful discussions, practically all the issues were closed, with the exception of the structural criteria of the electricity sector. The reality is that the strong impact of the oil shock resulted in the Government sacrificing more than RD 15,000 million from its coffers to subsidize this sector and avoid an adjustment of the electricity rate greater than authorized. However, I must emphasize and make it clear to public opinion and all economic agents, that the monetary targets were met with ample ease, in terms of Net Consolidated International Reserves and Net Domestic Assets. Additionally, the implementation of a fiscal adjustment plan allowed the deficit target to be met at the Central Government level, which registered an amount of RD 20,684 million at the end of June 2011, lower than the figure of RD 21,300 million established in the aforementioned Stand-by Agreement. This means that, from the macroeconomic point of view, and despite the difficult international conditions that the country has faced, the Government has done its homework. Similarly, by the end of September 2011 the monetary targets mentioned above are comfortably maintained, and the fiscal figures are in the process of final revision. As IDB President Luis Alberto Moreno noted during his recent visit to the country, when participating in the Twelfth Biarritz Forum, "a combined effort between monetary and fiscal policies, in addition to access to external resources in a timely manner, is required to counteract the effects of the turbulence present at the global level," recognizing the Dominican Republic. "as one of the model countries in handling the international crisis." In the same vein, the Ambassador of the European Union, Irene Horejs, stressed that "while the crisis is causing great havoc in the United States and Europe, the Dominican economy continues to grow above 4% with macroeconomic stability." But as the adage goes, "No one is a prophet in his land." Sector Real I would now like to refer to the recent performance of the economy in the Dominican Republic, as has been customary on this significant date for all Bancentralians. Allow me to announce to the country in this auditorium, the scoop that the Dominican economy in the period January-September 2011, measured through the Gross Domestic Product in real terms, experienced according to figures still very preliminary to date, a growth of 4.2%, behaviour that could well be considered satisfactory, given the prevailing adverse international situation. This result is within the estimate foreseen in the Monetary Program of the Central Bank in the context of the Agreement with the IMF, which contemplated a lower growth than that registered in the same period last year, given the need to moderate domestic demand and ensure that the economy grew according to its potential capacity in an environment of stability. A fact that I want to highlight and that has undoubtedly contributed to GDP growth this year, has been the recovery recorded by activities oriented to external demand, mainly free zones, which grew by 13.8% in January-September 2011, reversing their negative performance of -5.7% in the same period of 2010. In the same way, the growth of mining stands out by 73.9%, a sector of great potential for the year 2012, when ferronickel extractions will continue and the exploitation of gold will begin with high international prices. This should have a positive impact on a greater dynamization of Dominican exports, contributing to improving the terms of trade and the balance in the current account of the Balance of Payments. Another externally oriented sector that I want to highlight is tourism, as it is the main activity that generates foreign exchange in the country, and has a great impact on the rest of the economy. Many analysts had projected the collapse of this sector due to the effects of the global crisis, however it would seem that they did not take into consideration the emergence of new market niches or the success of Dominican promotional campaigns, since tourism, measured through the added value of hotels, bars and restaurants, grew 3.7% in January-September 2011. Ladies and gentlemen, the country has received in January-September 2011, some 3.3 million non-resident travelers for an increase of 111,469 additional foreigners, which indicates that our tourist offer maintains its attractiveness internationally. This result highlights the dynamism of the South American tourist flow, which in that period grew 42.6%, equivalent to 84,901 additional tourists mostly from Brazil, Argentina, Chile and Peru. Contrary to the negative estimates of some colleagues, the arrival of tourists from the United States increased by 40,345 additional passengers and although together those from Europe decreased by 14,813, mainly from Spain, England and Portugal, the entry of Russian tourists increased by 29,536 additional passengers, followed by France, Italy, Germany and Poland, which also increased their influx to the country. The other economic activities that make up the GDP, mostly showed growth in value added, highlighting local manufacturing 5.7%, agriculture 6.9%, financial intermediation and insurance 3.9%, trade 3.7%, education 5.3%, health 5.3% and other service activities 5.6%, representing together these activities 72.0% of GDP. Conversely, contractions were observed in energy and water (-6.9%) and communications (-1.7%) activities. At this point it is pertinent to highlight that the behavior of telecommunications collapsed the argument of some economists who claimed that Dominican economic growth was explained by the dynamism of cell phones. Well, friends, in the light of these results, I invite you to draw your own conclusions. On the other hand, I want to inform you that the sustained economic growth in the last seven years has had an impact on the creation of 714,286 net new jobs. This, together with the low levels of inflation and relative stability of the exchange rate, has resulted in a notable reduction in poverty levels by 11.8 percentage points in April 2011, standing at 31.6% in contrast to the high level of 43.4% existing in October 2004, according to calculations published by the Ministry of Economy, Planning and Development, using the World Bank's poverty methodology. This does not mean that we are denying the existence of a high level of poverty in our country, but we must recognize that although progress has been made in this regard, additional efforts are still required to reduce this terrible scourge, through policies to redistribute national income and targeted social programs that favor the most vulnerable segments of the population. Internal Prices I believe that these satisfactory economic results are an important factor in maintaining a climate of favourable confidence for investment, for which it has been key to maintain controlled inflation, despite the high international prices of oil and other primary goods that have caused inflationary pressures in all net importing countries of these goods. The Dominican Republic has been no exception. Indeed, during January-September 2011 accumulated inflation, measured by the variation of the Consumer Price Index (CPI), was 7.51%. In this regard, it is necessary to explain to the country that 81% of the growth of this index is due to the exogenous factors mentioned above, which caused increases in the prices of transportation, fuel, electricity, food and non-alcoholic beverages. As a sign that most of the inflation of the analyzed period responds to factors of external origin, it is verified that core inflation, which is attributable to monetary factors, stood at only 4.42% in the analyzed period. At this point I want to report that in September inflation was just 0.20%, mainly due to the reduction in international oil prices. External Sector Undoubtedly, dear friends, the behavior of the country's external transactions assumes great relevance in the current international economic situation. I recognize that the result of our current operations abroad has been an important concern, both of economic agents, analysts and business groups, which sometimes issue opinions without carefully weighing aspects that escape the domestic sphere, such as the effect of oil prices and certain commodities, of which we are importers. The preliminary figures of the external sector during the first nine months of the year, reflect that despite the unfavorable international outlook, total exports registered a notable increase of 24.4%, representing an additional US1,215.5 million compared to the same period of 2010. This growth has been driven mainly by mining, minor products and free zones, whose additional revenues significantly exceed the increase in the oil bill during that period. In the case of domestic exports of goods, their performance during the January-September period has been very positive, increasing by US650.3 million, thanks to the growth of exports of industrial origin, such as rum, beer, steel rods and gray cement, as well as and of agricultural origin, including bananas, avocados, peppers and peppers, highlighting exports to Haiti, a market that consumes about 50.0% of these products. In this regard, it is important to highlight the recovery of exports from free zones, especially footwear manufactures, medical and surgical equipment, jewelry and textiles, with an increase of US565.2 million over the amount recorded during January-September 2010, which reflects the favorable evolution of employment in this sector this year. It should be noted that during the period January-September 2011, in line with the moderation of the pace of growth of the economy and according to still very preliminary figures, total imports grew 16.7%, a significant slowdown of more than 10 percentage points compared to the 26.9% reached in the same period of 2010. In the same way, the growth of domestic imports has been reduced by almost half, going from 32.6% in January-September 2010 to 16.5% in the same period this year. It should be noted that of the total domestic imports, a third corresponded to the oil bill, amounting to US 3,448.2 million, higher by US 847.0 million than registered in 2010, due to the increase of 33.8% in the price of oil and its derivatives, even when the volume decreased by 2.4%. It is estimated that at the end of the year, the oil bill will exceed US 4 billion, an onerous burden for an economy like the Dominican one, which forces us to implement savings measures and look for alternative sources of energy generation, replacing expensive fuels with cheaper ones, such as natural gas, whose imported volume has increased by 15.6 percent. Although imported inflation hits economies such as the Dominican Republic, it should be noted that the favorable behavior of exports and other foreign exchange generating sectors contributed to the current account deficit in January-September ending with a growth of US 565.2 million. As can be seen, there has been a gradual improvement in this deficit on the side of increased exports and reduced imports. In addition, for tourism, in January-September they had entered some US 3,356.7 million, an increase of 3.7% over the same period last year, and remittances managed to reverse the reduction registered in January-September of last year, growing by 7.2% reaching an amount of US 2,356.5 million. These two items exceeded by US278.6 million the income received compared to the same period last year. As for the counterpart of the current balance, that is, the capital and financial account of the Balance of Payments, it obtained a positive result equivalent to US3,194.8 million, due to the significant inflow of external capital, thanks to the confidence of foreign investors in Dominican macroeconomic stability. This result has been influenced by the fact that during January-September of this year, US1,835.7 million entered foreign direct investment, for an increase of US397.4 million over the same period last year, estimating that by the end of the year it will exceed US2,000 million for the third consecutive year, a real feat considering the prevailing international context since the global crisis. In the same way, it should be noted that thanks to the macroeconomic stability, the positive prospects of the Dominican economy and the relatively low levels of country risk existing at that time, the Government was able to successfully place a sovereign bond for US500. million at a rate of 6.95%, the lowest financial cost of all the issues that the country has made since 2001. Definitely, this greater flow of foreign currency has favored the maintenance of net international reserve levels above the target established in the agreement with the IMF, as well as the relative stability of the exchange rate. Much has been debated in public opinion about the magnitude, sustainability and budgetary impact of Dominican public debt. Even some economists have gone so far as to argue that the country's borrowing capacity has already reached its limit. The reality is that most of these statements have been based on personal opinions, subjective criteria and partial information, without considering the macroeconomic context, nor addressing the problem with a long-term vision. Under any benchmark, the consolidated public debt of the Dominican Republic (which includes the Non-Financial Public Sector and the Rest of the Public Sector) is sustainable in the long term and its annual service is manageable in budgetary terms. At the end of August 2011, according to preliminary figures from the Ministry of Finance, Dominican consolidated public debt amounted to US21,112.1 million, equivalent to 37.9% of GDP estimated for this year and significantly lower than the 48.1% of GDP represented by debt in 2004. If we take as a reference the month of June 2011 to compare the Dominican consolidated public debt as a proportion of GDP with the main economies of the region, we have that it is below the average of most of these countries, some even more developed and competitive, such as: Brazil (66.1%), Mexico (42.7%), Argentina (47.8%), Costa Rica (44%) and Panama (40.9%). It should be remembered that some Latin American economies, such as Haiti, Bolivia, Honduras and Nicaragua are nations benefiting from the so-called Highly Indebted Poor Countries Initiative, known by its acronym in English as HIPC. These countries came to have a debt service of more than 20% to 25% of their export earnings and a debt stock equal to or greater than 250% of the country's export earnings, among other indicators, for which they benefited from special treatment, and currently only receive concessional credits, comprising terms of up to 40 years with interest rates of less than 1 per cent. Financial Sector Undoubtedly, dear friends, the high levels of capitalization, stability and solvency of the Dominican financial sector, are factors of strength to mitigate the adverse effects in the context of a strong international economic crisis. At the end of September 2011, in annualized terms, this sector showed a growth of its total assets of 11.7% and 32.4% for paid-in capital, with some banks registering a growth higher than these results. It should be noted that as of August of this year, all financial intermediaries had a solvency of 17.3%, much higher than the 10% established by the Monetary and Financial Law. In the same order, it should be noted that of the total loans granted by multiple banks at the end of September 2011, 91.2% were directed to the private sector, registering greater dynamism those granted to the manufacturing, communications, microenterprises, commerce, consumption and mining sectors. On the other hand, I must mention that the Monetary and Financial Administration, in line with the new Basel standards and best practices for risk-based supervision, has promoted the adaptation of the legislation that regulates the Financial System. In this regard, within the framework of the commitments assumed in the Stand-By Agreement with the International Monetary Fund, the National Congress is considering the Draft Amendment to the Monetary and Financial Law, as well as the one amending the Cheques Law, with a view to providing the country with a more modern legal framework adjusted to the new global schemes in this area. Likewise, the preparation of the Preliminary Draft Law on Financial and/or Economic Groups, which will establish the regulatory framework for consolidated supervision and prevention of systemic risk, is in the completion phase. Likewise, the Monetary Board approved the Project already converted into the Law for the Development of the Mortgage Market and the Trust, which proposes a range of new financial instruments that will boost the Securities Market, being in the final phase the issuance of its regulations. Institutional Developments Friends, allow me to take this important opportunity to share with you some of the main institutional advances that we have been making. I am pleased to announce that starting next year, the Central Bank of the Dominican Republic will officially adopt a monetary policy scheme based on an Inflation Targeting strategy, or Inflation Targeting as it is commonly known. In this sense, the Monetary Program will move from annual monetary aggregate targets to explicit inflation targets, subject to the mandate of the new Constitution and the Monetary and Financial Law that establish price stability as the central policy objective of this institution. Since 2005, the Central Bank began a process of gradual transition towards such a scheme, in accordance with the best practices of modern central banking. In fact, Latin American countries such as Mexico, Brazil, Chile, Peru, Colombia and Guatemala have been operating under this regime for several years quite successfully, which is based on the public announcement of a quantitative inflation target over a time horizon by the monetary authorities, which tends to anchor the expectations of market agents around that specific target. As part of this strategy, through monthly meetings, analysis and forecasting of the main international and local economic variables, the Central Bank uses its overnight rate to indicate to the market its monetary policy stance, complemented by a diverse range of monetary instruments to control the liquidity of the financial system and thus influence the domestic demand of the economy. in order to control inflation. In addition, the mechanisms for disseminating information of the Central Bank through its website have been strengthened, within the framework of transparency and access to information that characterizes the Central Bank, so that economic agents and the general public are duly built on monetary decisions and the prospects of the economy. Recently, the economic studies carried out by the Central Bank's technicians on various topics of a macro nature were circulated, as well as the beginning of the publication of the six-monthly Monetary Policy Report. Another element to highlight is that this Central Bank presented in February 2011 the results of the new CPI base December 2010, used to measure inflation. This involved the update of the consumption patterns of Dominicans, through a new family basket containing 305 goods and services distributed in twelve groups to calculate the CPI for each quintile. This project incorporates global best practices on the subject, for which technical assistance was received from several international experts, including the Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC). Likewise, I would like to reiterate the announcement I made recently that, as of 2012, the Central Bank will present the results of the national accounts with a change of base year corresponding to 2007, which will allow economic agents to have more up-to-date information on the national economy, given the structural changes that the Dominican productive apparatus has experienced. after facing two economic crises: internal and external. As for payment systems, we continue to walk the path of modernization and development. Since February of the current year, it initiated the System of Interconnection of Payments of Central America and the Dominican Republic (SIP), which allows the transfer of funds between customers of banks in Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua and the Dominican Republic, whose management is in charge of our Central Bank, in merit for having one of the most advanced electronic platforms, Safe and efficient in the region. I must also announce that a new Electronic Check Clearing House is in the implementation phase, which will reduce the time of bank transits to its minimum expression. On the other hand, as of January of this year, the securities of the Central Bank are placed in a dematerialized form, that is, physical certificates are no longer being issued, but they are represented by annotation in accounts, as modern international securities markets do. This means that it no longer matters the distance so that in real time, investors from Australia or Japan for example, can acquire and trade our securities. Similarly, at the end of this year, a new system will be implemented for conducting securities auctions electronically, which will make this mechanism much more efficient and secure, and the operations of Reports or Repos between financial intermediation entities will be modernized, using as underlying collateral, securities of the Central Bank and the Ministry of Finance. in order to deepen the interbank and public debt markets. As we see in recent years, our institution has been strengthened, incorporating the best standards, for which it has created the Office of Risk Management and Continuity. Similarly, in a relentless execution, the quasi-fiscal deficit of the Central Bank as a proportion of GDP has been significantly and consecutively, fully complying with the Recapitalization Law approved in 2007. Economic Outlook Dear friends, at a time when most international organizations are revising downwards the growth projections of most of the nations of the world, the Dominican Republic would be growing around 5% at the end of this year, with inflation estimated between 8 and 8.5%, explained by more than 70% by the prices of oil and key primary goods, as evidenced by the fact that core inflation would be around 5 percent. The truth is that it has been a titanic task, as I have repeated on several occasions, to have overcome the difficult international situation. And it is that maintaining the macroeconomic stability that the country currently enjoys has cost many hours of efforts of His Excellency Mr. President. of the Republic, Dr. Leonel Fernandez Reyna, the economic team and a series of officials and technicians from different public institutions at the service of the best national interests. Despite the unfavorable omens about the performance of the world economy, I still confess, at the expense of being stubborn, that I remain optimistic, because in the face of adversity there are also great opportunities for an economy like ours, which maintains comparative and competitive advantages in several sectors. Indeed, some of the primary goods that have registered increases in their international prices are produced in the country, such as gold, ferronickel, sugar, coffee and cocoa, among others. This, together with the boost of free zones, augurs encouraging prospects for our exports, in addition to the good performance of tourism, remittances and foreign investment. For sectors linked to domestic demand, we have favorable expectations that key activities such as agriculture, manufacturing and construction, just to name a few, will continue to grow. Precisely the construction sector, the one with the greatest multiplier effect, has great potential with the new Law on the Development of the Mortgage Market and the Trust, which will contribute to substantially reduce the housing deficit in the country, which will positively result in sustained economic growth, job creation and improvement of the quality of life of Dominican workers. Final Thoughts Friends, the complex international situation that affects us today is undeniable, because as the prominent economist Paul Krugman has said: "the economic crisis that began in 2008, is under no circumstances overcome". From the Central Bank we will continue to monitor this environment to act in a timely and proactive manner, as we have been doing, in order to contribute to mitigate its effects internally, and continue to fulfill our unavoidable commitment to maintain price stability. I am convinced that high and persistent levels of inflation generate uncertainty in the economy, to the detriment of economic growth, job creation and the well-being of the large social conglomerates of the population, which would be the most affected. A nation is like a balance, which in order to maintain equilibrium needs support, which is macroeconomic stability. Something that we have won, that we once lost, that we must take care of with great zeal, and that fortunately now in the pre-electoral period, the candidates have assumed the preservation of it as a key element in their government proposals. As I have emphatically pointed out in the scenarios where I have had the opportunity to speak, the challenges ahead are great. Dominicans have shown that we have the capacity to reinvent ourselves when necessary, with a creative and entrepreneurial spirit, assuming the private sector the leading role required to boost economic growth. We must make an effort so that our economic model is reoriented, having the integral development of the Human Being as its central axis, emphasizing education, health, decent housing and equal opportunities for all. In this regard, it is essential to promote domestic savings, investment, competitiveness, as well as greater and better national production that favors food security, among other priority and strategic tasks that allow us to continue on a path of progress and greater social equity. Paraphrasing that great technological entrepreneur recently disappeared, Steve Jobs, who was founder of Apple, I want to leave a message to the Bancentralian family: "everyone's time has limits ... have the courage to follow your heart and intuition... everything else is secondary." I conclude my words, as usual, exhorting you to bet on the future, with faith in God and optimism in a better future. May God bless you all! Thanks a lot. October 21st, 2011

Cabe recordar que algunas econom<92>as de Am<8e>rica Latina, como es el caso de Hait<92>, Bolivia, Honduras y Nicaragua son naciones beneficiadas por la llamada Iniciativa de Pa<92>ses Pobres Altamente Endeudados, conocida por sus siglas en ingl<8e>s como HIPC. Estos pa<92>ses llegaron a tener un servicio de deuda superior al 20% a 25% de sus ingresos por exportaciones y un stock de deuda igual o superior al 250% de los ingresos por exportaciones del pa<92>s, entre otros indicadores, por lo cual fueron beneficiados con un tratamiento especial, y en la actualidad s<97>lo reciben cr<8e>ditos concesionales, que comprenden plazos de hasta 40 a<96>os con tasas de inter<8e>s menores al 1 por ciento. Sector Financiero Sin lugar a dudas, apreciados amigos, los altos niveles de capitalizaci<97>n, la estabilidad y solvencia del sector financiero dominicano, constituyen factores de fortaleza para mitigar los efectos adversos en el contexto de fuerte crisis econ<97>mica internacional. Al cierre de septiembre 2011, en t<8e>rminos anualizados dicho sector exhibe un crecimiento de sus activos totales de 11.7% y de un 32.4% para el capital pagado, registrando algunos bancos un crecimiento superior a estos resultados. Debe ser destacado que a agosto del presente a<96>o, el conjunto de los intermediarios financieros presentaba una solvencia de 17.3%, muy superior al 10% que establece la Ley Monetaria y Financiera. En ese mismo orden debe destacarse, que del total de los pr<8e>stamos otorgados por los bancos m<9c>ltiples al cierre de septiembre de 2011, un 91.2% estuvo dirigido al sector privado, registrando mayor dinamismo los concedidos a los sectores manufactura, comunicaciones, microempresas, comercio, consumo y miner<92>a. Por otra parte, debo mencionar que la Administraci<97>n Monetaria y Financiera, en consonancia con los nuevos est<87>ndares de Basilea y mejores pr<87>cticas para una supervisi<97>n basada en riesgo, ha promovido la adecuaci<97>n de la legislaci<97>n que regula al Sistema Financiero. En ese orden cursa en el Congreso Nacional, en el marco de los compromisos asumidos en el Acuerdo Stand-By con el Fondo Monetario Internacional, el Proyecto de Modificaci<97>n de la Ley Monetaria y Financiera, as<92> como el que modifica la Ley de Cheques, con miras a dotar al pa<92>s de un marco legal m<87>s moderno y ajustado a los nuevos esquemas mundiales en la materia. Asimismo, se encuentra en fase de culminaci<97>n, la elaboraci<97>n del Anteproyecto de Ley de Grupos Financieros y/o Econ<97>micos, el cual establecer<87> el marco regulatorio para la supervisi<97>n consolidada y prevenci<97>n del riesgo sist<8e>mico. Igualmente, la Junta Monetaria aprob<97> el Proyecto ya convertido en la Ley para el Desarrollo del Mercado Hipotecario y el Fideicomiso, que plantea una gama de nuevos instrumentos financieros que impulsar<87>n al Mercado de Valores, encontr<87>ndose en fase final la emisi<97>n de sus reglamentos. Avances Institucionales Amigas y amigos, perm<92>tanme aprovechar esta importante ocasi<97>n para compartir con ustedes algunos de los principales avances institucionales que hemos venido alcanzando. Me es grato anunciarles que a partir del a<96>o pr<97>ximo, el Banco Central de la Rep<9c>blica Dominicana adoptar<87> de manera oficial un esquema de pol<92>tica monetaria basado en una estrategia de Metas de Inflaci<97>n, o Inflation Targeting como se conoce com<9c>nmente. En ese sentido, el Programa Monetario se mover<87> de metas anuales de agregados monetarios a metas expl<92>citas de inflaci<97>n, en sujeci<97>n al mandato de la nueva Constituci<97>n y de la Ley Monetaria y Financiera que establecen la estabilidad de precios como el objetivo central de pol<92>tica de esta Instituci<97>n. Desde el a<96>o 2005, el Banco Central inici<97> un proceso de transici<97>n gradual hacia dicho esquema, de acuerdo con las mejores pr<87>cticas de la banca central moderna. De hecho, pa<92>ses de Latinoam<8e>rica como M<8e>xico, Brasil, Chile, Per<9c>, Colombia y Guatemala tienen varios a<96>os operando bajo este r<8e>gimen con bastante <8e>xito, que se basa en el anuncio p<9c>blico de una meta cuantitativa de inflaci<97>n en un horizonte de tiempo por parte de las autoridades monetarias, lo cual tiende a anclar las expectativas de los agentes del mercado en torno a esa meta espec<92>fica. Como parte de esta estrategia, a trav<8e>s de reuniones mensuales, del an<87>lisis y pron<97>sticos de las principales variables econ<97>micas internacionales y locales, el Banco Central utiliza su tasa overnight para indicar al mercado su postura de pol<92>tica monetaria, complementado con una diversa gama de instrumentos monetarios para controlar la liquidez del sistema financiero y as<92> incidir en la demanda dom<8e>stica de la econom<92>a, a fin de controlar la inflaci<97>n. Adicionalmente, se han fortalecido los mecanismos de divulgaci<97>n de informaci<97>n del Banco Central a trav<8e>s de su p<87>gina Web, dentro del marco de transparencia y acceso a la informaci<97>n que caracteriza al Banco Central, de manera que los agentes econ<97>micos y el p<9c>blico en general est<8e>n debidamente edificados sobre las decisiones monetarias y las perspectivas de la econom<92>a. Recientemente se pusieron a circular los estudios econ<97>micos realizados por los t<8e>cnicos del Banco Central sobre diversos temas de car<87>cter macro, as<92> como el inicio de la publicaci<97>n del Informe de Pol<92>tica Monetaria de car<87>cter semestral. Otro elemento a destacar es que este Banco Central present<97> en el mes de febrero de 2011 los resultados del nuevo IPC base diciembre 2010, utilizado para medir la inflaci<97>n. Esto implic<97> la actualizaci<97>n de los patrones de consumo de los dominicanos, a trav<8e>s de una nueva canasta familiar que contiene 305 bienes y servicios distribuidos en doce grupos para calcular el IPC para cada quintil. Este proyecto incorpora las mejores pr<87>cticas mundiales sobre la materia, para lo cual se recibi<97> asistencia t<8e>cnica de varios expertos internacionales, incluyendo de la Comisi<97>n Econ<97>mica para Am<8e>rica Latina y el Caribe (CEPAL). Asimismo, me permito reiterarles el anuncio que hice recientemente de que, a partir del a<96>o 2012, el Banco Central presentar<87> los resultados de las cuentas nacionales con un cambio de a<96>o base correspondiente al 2007, que permitir<87> a los agentes econ<97>micos contar con informaciones m<87>s actualizadas de la econom<92>a nacional, dado los cambios estructurales que ha experimentado el aparato productivo dominicano, despu<8e>s de enfrentar dos crisis econ<97>micas: de origen interno y externo. En cuanto a los sistemas de pago, continuamos recorriendo el sendero de la modernizaci<97>n y el desarrollo. Desde febrero del a<96>o actual, inici<97> el Sistema de Interconexi<97>n de Pagos de Centroam<8e>rica y Rep<9c>blica Dominicana (SIP), que permite la transferencia de fondos entre los clientes de las entidades bancarias de Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua y Rep<9c>blica Dominicana, cuya gesti<97>n est<87> a cargo de nuestro Banco Central, en m<8e>rito por poseer una de las plataformas electr<97>nicas m<87>s avanzada, segura y eficiente de la regi<97>n. Asimismo, debo anunciar que est<87> en fase de implementaci<97>n una nueva C<87>mara de Compensaci<97>n Electr<97>nica de Cheques, que reducir<87> el tiempo de los tr<87>nsitos bancarios a su m<92>nima expresi<97>n. Por otra parte, a partir del mes de enero del presente a<96>o, los t<92>tulos-valores del Banco Central se colocan en forma desmaterializada, es decir, ya no se est<87>n emitiendo certificados f<92>sicos, sino que los mismos se representan mediante anotaci<97>n en cuentas, como lo hacen los mercados de valores internacionales modernos. Esto significa que ya no importa la distancia para que en tiempo real, inversionistas desde Australia o Jap<97>n por ejemplo, puedan adquirir y negociar nuestros t<92>tulos. De igual manera, a finales de este a<96>o, se implementar<87> un nuevo sistema para la realizaci<97>n de subastas de valores de forma electr<97>nica, que har<87> mucho m<87>s eficiente y seguro dicho mecanismo, y se modernizar<87>n las operaciones de Reportos o Repos entre las entidades de intermediaci<97>n financiera, utilizando como garant<92>a subyacente, valores del Banco Central y del Ministerio de Hacienda, en aras de profundizar los mercados interbancario y de deuda p<9c>blica. Como vemos en estos <9c>ltimos a<96>os se ha fortalecido nuestra instituci<97>n, incorporando los mejores est<87>ndares, para lo cual ha creado la Oficina de Gesti<97>n de Riesgo y Continuidad. De igual forma, en una ejecuci<97>n sin tregua, se ha logrado disminuir de manera significativa y consecutiva el d<8e>ficit cuasifiscal del Banco Central como proporci<97>n del PIB, cumpli<8e>ndose a la fecha a cabalidad la Ley de Recapitalizaci<97>n aprobada en el 2007. Perspectivas Econ<97>micas Apreciados amigos, en momentos en que la mayor<92>a de los organismos internacionales est<87>n revisando a la baja las proyecciones de crecimiento de la mayor<92>a de las naciones del mundo, la Rep<9c>blica Dominicana estar<92>a creciendo en torno al 5% al cierre del presente a<96>o, con una inflaci<97>n estimada entre 8 y 8.5%, explicada en m<87>s de un 70% por los precios del petr<97>leo y bienes primarios claves, como lo evidencia el hecho de que la inflaci<97>n subyacente estar<92>a en torno al 5 por ciento. La verdad es que ha sido una tarea tit<87>nica, como he repetido en varias ocasiones, haber sorteado la dif<92>cil situaci<97>n internacional. Y es que mantener la estabilidad macroecon<97>mica que disfruta actualmente el pa<92>s ha costado muchas horas de esfuerzos del Excelent<92>simo Se<96>or Presidente de la Rep<9c>blica, Dr. Leonel Fern<87>ndez Reyna, del equipo econ<97>mico y una serie de funcionarios y t<8e>cnicos de distintas instituciones p<9c>blicas al servicio de los mejores intereses nacionales. A pesar de los desfavorables augurios sobre el desempe<96>o de la econom<92>a mundial, todav<92>a les confieso, a expensas de pecar de testarudo, que mantengo mi optimismo, porque frente a la adversidad tambi<8e>n se presentan grandes oportunidades para una econom<92>a como la nuestra, que mantiene ventajas comparativas y competitivas en varios sectores. En efecto, algunos de los bienes primarios que han registrado alzas en sus precios internacionales se producen en el pa<92>s, como el caso del oro, ferron<92>quel, az<9c>car, caf<8e> y cacao, entre otros. Esto, junto al impulso de las zonas francas, augura alentadoras perspectivas para nuestras exportaciones, adem<87>s del buen desempe<96>o del turismo, las remesas y la inversi<97>n extranjera. Para los sectores vinculados a la demanda interna, tenemos expectativas favorables de que actividades claves como la agropecuaria, manufactura y construcci<97>n, por s<97>lo citar algunas, contin<9c>en creciendo. Precisamente al sector de la construcci<97>n, el de mayor efecto multiplicador, se le presentan grandes potencialidades con la nueva la Ley sobre el Desarrollo del Mercado Hipotecario y el Fideicomiso, que contribuir<87> a reducir sustancialmente el d<8e>ficit de viviendas en el pa<92>s, lo cual redundar<87> positivamente en el crecimiento econ<97>mico sostenido, en la generaci<97>n de empleo y en la mejor<92>a de la calidad de vida de los trabajadores dominicanos. Reflexiones Finales Amigas y amigos, es innegable la compleja situaci<97>n internacional que hoy nos afecta, pues como ha expresado el destacado economista Paul Krugman: <c7>la crisis econ<97>mica que inici<97> en 2008, no est<87> bajo ninguna circunstancia superada<c8>. Desde el Banco Central continuaremos monitoreando dicho entorno para actuar oportunamente y de forma proactiva, como lo hemos venido haciendo, a fin de contribuir a atenuar sus efectos a nivel interno, y continuar cumpliendo con nuestro compromiso ineludible de mantener la estabilidad de precios. Estoy convencido que niveles altos y persistentes de inflaci<97>n generan incertidumbre en la econom<92>a, en detrimento del crecimiento econ<97>mico, la creaci<97>n de empleos y el bienestar de los grandes conglomerados sociales de la poblaci<97>n, que ser<92>an los m<87>s afectados. Una naci<97>n es como una balanza, que para mantener el equilibrio necesita un soporte, que es la estabilidad macroecon<97>mica. Algo que hemos ganado, que una vez perdimos, que debemos cuidar con mucho celo, y que afortunadamente ahora en per<92>odo preelectoral, los candidatos han asumido la preservaci<97>n de la misma como un elemento clave en sus propuestas de gobierno. Como he se<96>alado de forma enf<87>tica en los escenarios en donde he tenido la oportunidad de disertar, son grandes los retos que tenemos por delante. Los dominicanos hemos demostrado que tenemos capacidad de reinventarnos cuando es necesario, con un esp<92>ritu creativo y emprendedor, asumiendo el sector privado el rol protag<97>nico que requiere el impulso del crecimiento econ<97>mico. Debemos hacer un esfuerzo para que nuestro modelo econ<97>mico se reoriente, teniendo al desarrollo integral del Ser Humano como su eje central, enfatizando la educaci<97>n, la salud, la vivienda digna y la igualdad de oportunidades para todos. En ese tenor, es fundamental promover el ahorro interno, la inversi<97>n, la competitividad, al igual que una mayor y mejor producci<97>n nacional que favorezca la seguridad alimentaria, entre otras tareas prioritarias y estrat<8e>gicas que nos permitan seguir transitando por un sendero de progreso y mayor equidad social. Parafraseando a ese gran emprendedor tecnol<97>gico recientemente desaparecido, Steve Jobs, quien fuera fundador de Apple, quiero dejar un mensaje a la familia bancentraliana: <c7>el tiempo de todos tiene l<92>mites<c9> tengan el valor de seguir su coraz<97>n e intuici<97>n... todo lo dem<87>s es secundario<c8>. Finalizo mis palabras, como de costumbre, exhort<87>ndolos a que apostemos al futuro, con fe en Dios y optimismo en un mejor porvenir. <c1>Que Dios los bendiga a todos! Muchas gracias. 21 de octubre, 2011

Title: Speech at the XI Regional Conference on Central America, Panama and the Dominican Republic
CentralBank: Central Bank of the Dominican Republic
text: CENTRAL BANK OF THE DOMINICAN REPUBLIC WELCOME WORDS XI REGIONAL CONFERENCE ON CENTRAL AMERICA, PANAMA AND THE DOMINICAN REPUBLIC 26 and 27 July 2012 Hard Rock Hotel, Punta Cana Hector Valdez Albizu Governor On behalf of the Government and the Monetary, Financial and Fiscal Authorities of the Dominican Republic, allow me to extend a warm welcome to this beautiful Caribbean island. It is a great privilege and a real pleasure for us to host the Eleventh Annual Regional Conference on Central America, Panama and the Dominican Republic, hosted by the International Monetary Fund. On behalf of the Central Bank and myself, I want to express our deep gratitude for having taken time out of your busy schedules to join us in this event that has as its main stage, the wonderful tourist enclave of Punta Cana. Undoubtedly, we are in the right place to generate a true space for dialogue and policy agreement, in the company of the main monetary, fiscal and financial authorities of the region, as well as prominent representatives of multilateral organizations. And it is precisely in the current moments of global uncertainty, when this type of exercise becomes more important, since it allows us to evaluate the risks, perspectives and challenges posed by the international economic and financial environment, as well as its potential impact on the well-being of our region. Just at the moment that we seemed to be witnessing a definitive recovery of the world economy, the Eurozone has been affected by a worsening of its fiscal and debt crisis, to the point that some economists such as Nobel Prize winner Paul Krugman, have come to warn about the possibility of a new recessionary round in the world economy and about the challenges faced by countries to consolidate the Euro as a currency. international. In this context, the latest estimates of world growth for 2012 have been revised downwards again, with the International Monetary Fund projecting an expansion of 3.5% and the Economic Consensus, a more pessimistic scenario, around 2.5%. The lack of agreement on the specific policies to be adopted to face the European crisis has been decisive in the downward revision of growth projections. Both the IMF and the Economic Consensus currently maintain a mild recession forecast for the Eurozone, with risks skewed to the downside. In this scenario, the impact of the European crisis on the American continent is expected to be moderate, with the United States and Latin America growing in 2012 at around 2.0% and 3.4%, respectively. Faced with such a complex international environment, our region must join forces for true fiscal consolidation to improve debt sustainability, while continuing to strengthen the institutional framework of monetary policy, as have some countries in the region that have adopted or are in a transition phase towards an inflation-targeting scheme. Likewise, we must continue to advance in the implementation of macro-prudential policies that serve as a safeguard against the deterioration of international financial conditions. There is no doubt that the institutions represented here, Ministries of Finance, Central Banks and Superintendencies of Financial and Securities Institutions, among others, have a great challenge as interlocutors and facilitators of prudential reorganization, institutional strengthening and the development and deepening of financial and capital markets. But, I ask you, dear friends, what are these policies worth if we do not achieve with them, an effective reduction of our poverty levels? Hence, the importance of designing and implementing social programmes that are part of a comprehensive development strategy, aimed at strengthening State institutions, increasing the productivity and competitiveness of our economies and promoting international trade. Fortunately, growth prospects for the countries of Central America and the Caribbean, as for the rest of Latin America, remain encouraging. We must use this incentive to continue laying the foundations for stronger growth in the future, avoiding, as on other occasions, "resting on our laurels". It is my opinion, friends, that this XI Regional Conference offers us a privileged opportunity to exchange ideas and discuss possible strategies that will allow us to make this growth sustainable in an unfavorable international environment. In the Dominican Republic we are willing to make this commitment our own, because we know that sustained growth and macroeconomic stability require effort and sacrifice, as well as a vision of a nation that must be supported from the highest levels of government. In that regard, allow me to take this opportunity to thank His Excellency the President of the Republic, Leonel Fernandez Reyna, for his unrestricted support and his unwavering commitment to the basic principles of a healthy economy. Without this commitment, the Dominican Republic would not have been able to overcome the international crisis with relative success and maintain, despite the difficult global environment, healthy growth with low inflation. Dear friends, the holding of this Regional Conference in the country coincides with the period of transition towards a new State administration. In the coming days, the chemical engineer and economist, Danilo Medina, will assume the first magistracy of the Dominican Republic. The President-elect has repeatedly expressed his commitment to macroeconomic stability, which, in his view, is an indispensable condition for achieving sustained growth that allows a redistribution aimed at improving the living conditions of all Dominicans. In conclusion, I would like to sincerely thank you for the participation of such a distinguished audience in this regional conference, as well as wish you a pleasant stay in our beautiful country. I would like to thank in particular the Governors and Presidents of Central Banks, Ministers and Superintendents, together with their companions, as well as the IMF, in the figure of its Deputy Director-Manager, Mr. Min Zhu, and the prestigious group of exhibitors who will be accompanying us during this important activity. Let us therefore continue with our line of cooperation, planning and forecasting, so that together we can achieve the design of a true reform of the regional financial apparatus and its respective regulatory structures. Without further ado, and taking this opportunity to wish the greatest success in this commendable work that concerns us, I wish you all a successful day of work both today and tomorrow, as well as a pleasant stay in this beautiful environment with which we have been blessed. Be all once again welcome to the Dominican Republic and feel at home. Thanks a lot.
text_original: BANCO CENTRAL DE LA REP<f2>BLICA DOMINICANA PALABRAS DE BIENVENIDA XI CONFERENCIA REGIONAL SOBRE CENTROAMERICA, PANAMA Y LA REPUBLICA DOMINICANA 26 y 27 de julio de 2012 Hard Rock Hotel, Punta Cana Lic. H<8e>ctor Valdez Albizu Gobernador En nombre del Gobierno y de las Autoridades Monetarias, Financieras y Fiscales de la Rep<9c>blica Dominicana, perm<92>tanme darles la m<87>s cordial bienvenida a esta hermosa isla del Caribe. Es para nosotros un gran privilegio y un verdadero placer ser los anfitriones de la Decimoprimera Conferencia Regional Anual sobre Centroam<8e>rica, Panam<87> y la Rep<9c>blica Dominicana, auspiciada por el Fondo Monetario Internacional. En nombre del Banco Central y del m<92>o propio, quiero expresarles nuestra profunda gratitud por haber sacado tiempo de sus apretadas agendas para acompa<96>arnos en este evento que tiene como escenario principal, el maravilloso enclave tur<92>stico de Punta Cana. Sin lugar a dudas nos encontramos en el lugar propicio para generar un verdadero espacio de di<87>logo y concertaci<97>n de pol<92>ticas, en compa<96><92>a de las principales autoridades monetarias, fiscales y financieras de la regi<97>n, as<92> como de destacados representantes de organismos multilaterales. Y es precisamente en los actuales momentos de incertidumbre global, cuando este tipo de ejercicio cobra mayor importancia, ya que nos permite evaluar los riesgos, perspectivas y desaf<92>os que nos plantea el entorno econ<97>mico y financiero internacional, as<92> como su potencial impacto en el bienestar de nuestra regi<97>n. Justo en el momento que parec<92>amos asistir a una recuperaci<97>n definitiva de la econom<92>a mundial, la Zona Euro se ha visto afectada por un recrudecimiento de su crisis fiscal y de deuda, hasta el punto de que algunos economistas como el Premio Nobel Paul Krugman, han llegado a alertar sobre la posibilidad de una nueva ronda recesiva en la econom<92>a mundial y sobre los retos que enfrentan los pa<92>ses para consolidar el Euro como divisa internacional. En este contexto, las <9c>ltimas estimaciones del crecimiento mundial para 2012 han sido revisadas nuevamente a la baja, proyectando el Fondo Monetario Internacional una expansi<97>n de 3.5% y el Consenso Econ<97>mico, un escenario m<87>s pesimista, en torno a 2.5%. La falta de un acuerdo en cuanto a las pol<92>ticas espec<92>ficas a ser adoptadas para enfrentar la crisis europea, ha sido determinante en la revisi<97>n a la baja de las proyecciones de crecimiento. Tanto el FMI como el Consenso Econ<97>mico, mantienen en la actualidad un pron<97>stico de recesi<97>n leve para la Zona Euro, con riesgos sesgados a la baja. En este escenario, se espera que el impacto de la crisis europea sobre el continente Americano sea moderado, creciendo Estados Unidos y Am<8e>rica Latina en 2012 en torno a 2.0% y 3.4%, respectivamente. Ante un entorno internacional tan complejo, nuestra regi<97>n debe aunar esfuerzos para una verdadera consolidaci<97>n fiscal que permita mejorar la sostenibilidad de la deuda, al tiempo que se continua fortaleciendo la institucionalidad de la pol<92>tica monetaria, tal y como lo han hecho algunos pa<92>ses de la regi<97>n que han adoptado o que se encuentran en una fase de transici<97>n hacia un esquema de metas de inflaci<97>n. De igual forma, debemos seguir avanzando en la implementaci<97>n de pol<92>ticas macro-prudenciales que sirvan de resguardo ante el deterioro de las condiciones financieras internacionales. Es indudable que las instituciones aqu<92> representadas, Ministerios de Hacienda, Bancos Centrales y Superintendencias de Instituciones Financieras y de Valores, entre otros, tienen un gran reto como interlocutores y facilitadores del reordenamiento prudencial, del fortalecimiento institucional y del desarrollo y profundizaci<97>n de los mercados financieros y de capitales. Pero, les pregunto estimados amigos <c0>De qu<8e> valen estas pol<92>ticas si no logramos con ellas, una efectiva reducci<97>n de nuestros niveles de pobreza? De ah<92>, la importancia del dise<96>o y ejecuci<97>n de programas sociales que se enmarquen dentro de una estrategia de desarrollo comprehensiva, orientada a fortalecer las instituciones del Estado, a incrementar la productividad y la competitividad de nuestras econom<92>as y a promover el comercio internacional. Afortunadamente, las perspectivas de crecimiento para los pa<92>ses de Centroam<8e>rica y el Caribe, al igual que para el resto de Am<8e>rica Latina, siguen siendo alentadoras. Debemos usar este aliciente para continuar sentando las bases de un crecimiento m<87>s s<97>lido en el futuro, evitando, como en otras ocasiones, <d2>dormirnos en nuestro laureles<d3>. Es mi opini<97>n, amigos y amigas, que esta XI Conferencia Regional nos ofrece una oportunidad privilegiada para intercambiar ideas y discutir posibles estrategias que nos permitan hacer sostenible este crecimiento en un entorno internacional desfavorable. En Rep<9c>blica Dominicana estamos dispuestos a hacer nuestro este compromiso, pues sabemos que el crecimiento sostenido y la estabilidad macroecon<97>mica requieren de esfuerzo y sacrificio, as<92> como de una visi<97>n de naci<97>n que debe ser respaldada desde las mas altas instancias del Gobierno. Estimados amigos, la celebraci<97>n de esta Conferencia Regional en el pa<92>s coincide con el periodo de transici<97>n hacia una nueva administraci<97>n del Estado. Para finalizar, deseo agradecer sinceramente la participaci<97>n de tan distinguida audiencia en esta conferencia regional, as<92> como desearles una agradable estad<92>a en nuestro bello pa<92>s. Gobernadores y Presidentes de Bancos Centrales, Ministros y Superintendentes, junto a sus acompa<96>antes, as<92> como al FMI, en la figura de su Subdirector-Gerente, el Sr. Min Zhu, y al prestigioso grupo de expositores que nos estar<87> acompa<96>ando durante esta importante actividad. Continuemos pues con nuestra l<92>nea de cooperaci<97>n, planificaci<97>n y previsi<97>n, para as<92> entre todos lograr el dise<96>o de una verdadera reforma del aparato financiero regional y sus respectivas estructuras de regulaci<97>n.
